surfaces.name: The roof API

projects.what: A transistor-level MOS 6502 traced from die photographs, and everything built on it: the explorer, the API over the real chip, the warm engine process and the console.

surfaces.name: The explorer
surfaces.what: The die itself, lit by what it is doing, plus the measured tables and the primer.

surfaces.name: The long reads
surfaces.what: Every tool's prose as an article, listed longest first: what each instrument is doing, written to be read end to end rather than operated.

surfaces.name: The 6502 API
surfaces.what: A transistor-level MOS 6502 over HTTP, one half-cycle at a time. The reference checks itself against the running service.
surfaces.status: here; the subdomain still answers too, until the forward (notes/forward.md)

surfaces.name: Die Runner
surfaces.what: Die Runner: a console whose frames are run on the real die. The builder pages and the cartridge editor live beside it.

surfaces.name: The editor
surfaces.what: Claim a handle, edit your page, publish a ROM: the registry's writing half, signed in with your token.

surfaces.name: The registry
surfaces.what: Everyone publishing cartridges, and what they published.

surfaces.name: The halfwave lab
surfaces.what: A 6502, half a clock phase at a time. The research bench, and it stays one.

surfaces.name: The visual6502 archive
surfaces.what: visual6502.org recovered from the Wayback Machine, 174 MB of it: the wiki rebuilt from its wikitext and the die photography made browsable again.

projects.name: hotbits
projects.what: True random bytes from the decay of a radioactive source: a Geiger counter on a Pi, with bits taken from the timing between decay events.

surfaces.name: The entropy gateway
surfaces.what: Keys and byte budgets in front of the TRNG. /v1/bytes needs a bearer token; /v1/seeds needs no key and cannot drain the pool. The open /random/* endpoints answer 410 and say why: the pool refills at a few dozen bytes a minute and was reachable by anyone.

surfaces.name: The Geiger TRNG
surfaces.what: The instrument itself, and what it has measured: the byte pool, the randomness batteries, long-term and diurnal series, incidents and sensors.

projects.name: The NES console
projects.what: A working NES built from our own parts: both chips simulated switch by switch, every connection between them checked against recorded reference runs, and a picture path already tested on a real console.

surfaces.name: The console arc
surfaces.what: What the console is, where each part of it lives, and what still waits on the real hardware.

surfaces.name: Play
surfaces.what: The console from the repository running in the page: both fast chips, the sound, and the signal path's three-line comb, on a cartridge from your own disk.

surfaces.name: Create
surfaces.what: The console from the play page with every tool for looking inside a game on one desk: the code, the CPU, the memory, the palettes, the sprites and the sprite editor, as windows you arrange.

surfaces.name: The NES at human speed
surfaces.what: The console's model slowed down until a person can watch it: the beam drawing a frame, the line as volts on the wire, a real game's frame measured, the pad read a bit at a time, and the picture chip running transistor by transistor.

surfaces.name: The chips
surfaces.what: The contract every chip speaks, the 2A03 and the 2C02 at their switches, and the fast chips built from them. Every figure comes from re-running the chip repositories' own tests.

surfaces.name: The console
surfaces.what: Both chips on one board and one clock, then the picture through the television model, the sound through the board's audio stage, and the window it plays in.

surfaces.name: The signal
surfaces.what: The composite video signal itself, simulated sample by sample: encoded from three sources, pulled apart by four different filters and shown through a five-stage CRT model, with a check that can fail at every stage.

surfaces.name: The signal bench
surfaces.what: The signal path running in your browser: NES dots encoded to the composite waveform and decoded by the filter you choose, with the drift counters visible.

surfaces.name: Composite, terminated
surfaces.what: A real NES's composite video read off the scope into the 75 ohms it was built to drive: the scanline, the burst, the levels beside the transcribed table, and what measuring without the terminator had made look bigger.

surfaces.name: The bench
surfaces.what: A real console and the model under the same controller presses: the bridge between them as drawn and as built, and what has happened at the bench so far.

surfaces.name: The calibration cart
surfaces.what: One cartridge of our own whose every screen is built to be measured, off a real console and off the model through the same decoder. The plan, the build, the screens and the blank boards.

surfaces.name: The console arc's notebook
surfaces.what: Every plan and report for the console, grouped by the part they are about: the chips, the signal, the console and the bench. The repositories are the one copy; this site pulls them at build time.

surfaces.name: The console arc, in retrospect
surfaces.what: What the sketch asked for, what the chips and the ROMs taught, and what stays for a bench.
